title: Can a robot camera calibrate itself without a checkerboard, and does it know when it is wrong?
lede: research programme on target-free camera self-calibration; milestone 1 on two real cameras: bundle adjustment with the board's geometry withheld lands within 0.15% and 0.24% of Zhang's focal length from a 30% wrong start, with a σ only 1.12× Zhang's; its free 3-D corners show the board itself bends (0.8% of a square rms, same shape from both cameras, r 0.90); over 400 view subsets both solvers' σ is about 2× too small
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) on recalibrating a camera from the features it already sees, with no target, and on whether the solver's own uncertainty is honest enough for a robot to accept or reject the update. Milestone 1 uses OpenCV's real stereo calibration photos (two cameras, 13 views each, Apache-2.0): the checkerboard corners are kept as correspondences but the board's geometry is withheld, so the 54 corners become free 3-D points. Started 30% off in focal length, bundle adjustment lands at 534.8 and 538.4 px against Zhang's 535.6 and 539.7 px (gaps 0.15% and 0.24%, under 1σ), with a reported σ 1.12× Zhang's, refuting our prediction of a 2× price for having no target. The free corners leave their best plane by 0.0077 square widths rms (0.024 at most), and the two cameras, solved separately, reconstruct the same bend (correlation 0.90; 0.91 with a second distortion term): the printed board is not flat, which a flat-board model cannot absorb (target-free reprojection error 0.26 against 0.42 px). Over 400 random subsets of 3 to 12 views the focal length's z-score against the all-view reference has rms 1.94 (95% 1.75–2.12) for 4–12 views, so the reported σ is about twice too small; Zhang's is no better (2.16). Limits: one rig and board, corners without mismatches, the reference is itself a flat-board fit, and every solve stopped on its evaluation cap.
